key_terms.meaning: A small grid of learnable weights, say 3×3, that is slid over the input; at each position it gives one dot product plus bias.
The 2-D output of convolving one kernel over the whole input; large values mark where that kernel's pattern occurs.
Number of pixels the kernel moves per step; stride 2 roughly halves the output height and width.
Extra rows and columns, usually zeros, added around the input so the kernel can cover border pixels and the output size can be controlled.
Replace each small window (say 2×2) by its maximum, shrinking the map and keeping only the strongest response.
The elementwise non-linearity max(0, x); it keeps positive values and turns negatives into zero.
During training, randomly set a fraction of activations to zero so the network cannot rely on single units.
An 8-layer CNN (5 convolution layers, 3 fully connected) that won the 2012 ImageNet challenge using ReLU and dropout.
The 2013 ImageNet winner: AlexNet with a smaller first-layer stride and smaller first-layer kernels, chosen by looking at learned features.
An architecture built only from 3×3 convolutions stacked in blocks with 2×2 max pooling; 16-layer and 19-layer versions are common.
Several branches (1×1, 3×3, 5×5 convolutions and 3×3 max pooling) run on the same input and their outputs are concatenated.
An identity shortcut that adds the block input to its output, y = F(x) + x, so gradients reach early layers in very deep nets.
Start from weights trained on a large dataset (for example ImageNet) and adapt them to a new task with less data and compute.
The final fully connected layers that turn features into class scores; usually replaced with a new head for the new task.
Unfreezing some pretrained layers and continuing training on the new data with a small learning rate.
A convolution run in the reverse direction that maps a feature map back up to pixel space.
Gradient ascent on the input image itself, increasing whatever the network already detects so patterns are amplified.
Weights each channel of the last convolution feature map by the gradient of a class score, giving a coarse heat map of important regions.
Detection as one regression: an S×S grid where each cell predicts box coordinates, an objectness score and class probabilities.
Two identical subnetworks with the same parameters applied to two inputs, as in a Siamese network.

takeaways: Convolution replaces hand-written features with kernels whose weights are learned, and the feature map records where a pattern was found.
Stride and padding are the two dials that set the output size of every convolution layer.
Pooling shrinks the map and buys small translation tolerance, while ReLU supplies the non-linearity that convolution alone lacks.
A basic CNN is just a stack of convolution–ReLU–pool blocks ending in a flatten and a few fully connected layers.
AlexNet, ZFNet and VGG showed that depth, ReLU, dropout and small 3×3 kernels beat hand-designed image features.
Inception widens a layer by running several kernel sizes in parallel; ResNet goes deep by adding identity shortcuts that keep gradients alive.
Transfer learning lets a small team with one GPU and a few thousand images reuse ImageNet features instead of training from scratch.
Visualization methods such as deconvolution, DeepDream and Grad-CAM turn a trained CNN from a black box into something you can inspect.
Detection answers what and where: R-CNN-style methods propose regions then classify, YOLO does both in a single forward pass.
Segmentation labels every pixel, and Siamese networks reuse one network twice to answer same-or-different.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine a correct numeric shape/dimension calculation with a clear account of how architectures evolved and what each design change fixed, so keep layer tables and comparisons ready.

bank.q: Explain the convolution operation on a 2-D image with a single kernel. Define kernel, stride and padding, and state the formula for the output size.
outline: Convolution slides a kernel over the input and takes the sum of elementwise products plus a bias at each position
Define kernel size, stride and zero padding with symbols
Output size formula: H_out = (H_in + 2P − K)/S + 1, with each term defined
A worked small example showing one dot product and one border position
Why the same kernel is reused at every position (weight sharing) and what the resulting feature map means

bank.q: Describe max pooling and the role of non-linear activation functions in a CNN. Why is pooling useful after a convolution layer?
outline: Definition of pooling window, stride of pooling, and the max/average variants
Effect on feature map size and on the number of parameters
Pooling keeps the strongest response and gives small translation tolerance
ReLU formula max(0, x) and why it trains faster than sigmoid/tanh
Without a non-linearity a stack of convolutions is still a linear map

bank.q: Draw and describe the AlexNet architecture layer by layer. Point out where ReLU, dropout and data augmentation are used and why.
outline: Input 224×224×3 (with padding/cropping as done in the original)
Five convolution layers with kernel sizes and channel counts, max pooling after some of them
Three fully connected layers ending in 1000 softmax outputs
ReLU after every convolution and fully connected layer
Dropout in the fully connected layers to reduce overfitting; augmentation of the training images
Why it mattered: large margin of improvement over hand-designed features on ImageNet

bank.q: What is transfer learning for CNNs? Distinguish feature extraction from fine-tuning and state when you would use each.
outline: Pretrained model and the convolution base versus the classifier head
Feature extraction: freeze the base, train only the new head
Fine-tuning: unfreeze the top blocks of the base and train with a small learning rate
Small dataset and very different images: extract features or fine-tune few layers
Large dataset: fine-tune more layers
Always replace and retrain the classifier head to match the new number of classes

bank.q: An input of size 32×32×3 passes through: conv 3×3, 16 filters, stride 1, padding 1; then 2×2 max pooling; then conv 3×3, 32 filters, stride 1, padding 0. Compute the output shape after each stage and the number of weights in each convolution layer.
outline: Use H_out = (H_in + 2P − K)/S + 1 at every stage
After conv1: 32×32×16
After pooling: 16×16×16
After conv2: 14×14×32
Weights of a convolution layer = K × K × C_in × C_out, plus C_out biases

bank.q: Design a basic CNN for 10-class classification of 32×32 colour images. Give a layer table with output shapes and justify each design choice.
outline: Two or three blocks of conv–ReLU–pool, increasing filters (for example 32, 64, 128)
Padding and stride stated numerically so shapes are reproducible
Flatten or global average pooling into a vector
One or two fully connected layers with dropout, then 10-way softmax
Cross-entropy loss, parameter count estimate, and why pooling reduces compute
Mention data augmentation as a cheap regulariser

bank.q: You have 4,000 labelled images of Indian traffic signs in 20 classes and a pretrained ImageNet model. Write a step-by-step fine-tuning plan with learning rates, frozen layers and evaluation.
outline: Replace the classifier head with a 20-way head
Stage 1: freeze the convolution base, train the head with a normal learning rate
Stage 2: unfreeze the last block or two, use a learning rate 10–100× smaller
Keep batch normalisation layers frozen or in inference mode while fine-tuning
Split train/validation/test, use augmentation, monitor overfitting
Report accuracy and per-class confusion; compare against training from scratch on the same data

bank.q: Explain how YOLO turns detection into a regression problem. For an S×S grid with B boxes and C classes, write the shape of the output tensor and the terms of the loss.
outline: Image divided into an S×S grid; the cell containing an object's centre is responsible for it
Each cell predicts B boxes, each with x, y, w, h and a confidence score
Per-cell class probabilities of length C
Output tensor shape S × S × (B×5 + C)
Loss = localisation error on responsible boxes + confidence error for object/no-object cells + classification error
NMS at test time; speed versus region-proposal methods

bank.q: Compare AlexNet, ZFNet and VGG on kernel sizes, depth, parameter count and what each contributed to CNN design.
outline: AlexNet: large 11×11 and 5×5 first kernels, 8 layers, ReLU and dropout
ZFNet: smaller first-layer kernel and stride, chosen by inspecting feature visualisations; showed visualization can guide design
VGG: only 3×3 convolutions, deeper stacks, uniform blocks; two 3×3 layers have the same receptive field as one 5×5 but fewer weights and more non-linearity
Parameter explosion in the fully connected layers of VGG
Depth plus small kernels gave steady error reduction on ImageNet
Trade-off between accuracy and inference cost

bank.q: Why does adding more plain convolution layers eventually make training worse? Explain the Inception module and the ResNet residual block as two answers to that problem.
outline: Degradation problem: deeper plain nets show higher training error, not just overfitting
Vanishing gradients and difficulty of learning an identity map through many layers
Inception: parallel 1×1, 3×3, 5×5 convolutions and pooling, concatenated; 1×1 layers reduce channel count before expensive kernels
ResNet: block learns residual F(x) and output is F(x) + x; identity is easy to represent
Shortcut gives a direct path for gradients; use of batch normalisation
Result: networks of 50–150+ layers train and improve accuracy

bank.q: Compare deconvolution-based feature visualisation, DeepDream and Grad-CAM as ways of opening the CNN black box. What does each reveal and what are its limits?
outline: Deconvolution/transposed convolution maps activations back to pixel space to show which pattern a filter responds to
DeepDream performs gradient ascent on the input, amplifying existing patterns; good for intuition, not a faithful explanation
Grad-CAM uses class-score gradients on the last conv map for a coarse localisation heat map; class-specific and cheap
Limits: coarse resolution, not a proof of causal reasoning, visualisations can be cherry-picked
Best practice: use them together and sanity-check with occlusion or ablation

bank.q: Contrast R-CNN-style detectors with YOLO on accuracy, speed and pipeline complexity. Where would you choose each in a real deployment?
outline: R-CNN: region proposals, then CNN features per proposal, then SVM/regressor; slow and multi-stage
Fast/Faster R-CNN: share convolution, add ROI pooling and a region proposal network to cut cost
YOLO: single network, single pass, grid regression, real-time but weaker on small or crowded objects
Metrics: mAP, IoU threshold, frames per second
Memory and hardware: edge device versus server
Choice depends on latency budget, object size and how much labelled data exists

bank.q: You must build a system that finds potholes in street photos from a phone, with 2,000 labelled images and one GPU. Justify your choices of pretrained model, transfer-learning strategy, detection head and evaluation plan.
outline: Why training from scratch is not viable with 2,000 images; use an ImageNet-pretrained base
Feature extraction first, then fine-tune the top blocks with a small learning rate
Use a detection formulation (boxes) rather than plain classification, or a segmentation mask if pixel area matters
Input resolution, augmentation, class imbalance and background images
Validation split, mAP or IoU-based metric, per-condition error analysis
Deployment cost, inference speed on a phone, and how to inspect failures using Grad-CAM or feature visualisation

glossary.def: An operation that slides a kernel over an input and computes a dot product at every position to build a feature map.
A small matrix of learnable weights applied by convolution.
The output grid produced by one kernel over the whole input.
The step size, in pixels, by which the kernel moves between positions.
Border rows and columns added to the input, usually zeros, to control output size.
The region of the original input that a given neuron's value depends on.
A downsampling operation that keeps the maximum value in each window.
Averaging each feature map to one number, often used instead of a flatten layer.
The activation max(0, x) applied elementwise.
A function that turns a vector of scores into probabilities that sum to 1.
Reshaping a 3-D feature map into a 1-D vector before fully connected layers.
Randomly zeroing activations during training to reduce overfitting.
Normalising layer inputs by batch mean and variance, then scaling and shifting with learned parameters.
Using the same weights at every spatial position, which is what makes convolution cheap.
The 2012 ImageNet-winning 8-layer CNN that popularised ReLU and dropout for vision.
The 2013 ImageNet winner, a tuned AlexNet guided by feature visualisation.
A deep CNN family built from repeated 3×3 convolutions and max pooling.
A block that runs several kernel sizes in parallel and concatenates their outputs.
A block whose output is F(x) + x through an identity shortcut.
Reusing knowledge, in practice weights, learned on one task for another task.
Continuing training of pretrained layers on new data, usually with a small learning rate.
A transposed convolution that maps a feature map back towards image space.
An image generated by gradient ascent on the input to amplify patterns the network detects.
A class-specific heat map built from gradients flowing into the last convolution layer.
A candidate bounding box suggested before classification in R-CNN-style detectors.
Two copies of one network with shared weights that produce embeddings for two inputs to compare them.
A loss that pulls embeddings of similar pairs together and pushes dissimilar pairs apart by a margin.
Assigning a class label to every pixel of an image.
